71.title: The changed word
71.hook: his son Ram Rai alters a word of Nanak's hymn to please the court, and the Guru refuses to see him again
71.howItsDone: Sikhs hold that the words of the Guru Granth Sahib must never be altered; the story of Ram Rai is told as the example of what happens when the word is changed to please power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dara Shikoh, the emperor's son cured with medicine from the garden. Your line was heal whoever asks.

You're in a meeting with the most powerful person you've ever met. They quote something your grandmother used to say, and ask what it means. The honest answer might annoy them; you can see it in their face. So you shade it. Just one word, just enough to keep the room happy. It even has a polite name: being diplomatic. Now change two things. The thing you shaded wasn't your grandmother's saying. It was scripture. And the powerful person was the emperor. Today, the gentle seventh Guru draws the hardest line of his life, against his own son, over a single word.
screen: `THE MOST POWERFUL PERSON IN THE ROOM.` → `JUST ONE WORD, SHADED.` → `AND IT WAS SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: By 1661 there was a new emperor, Aurangzeb, who had fought his way to the throne, and he summoned Guru Har Rai to Delhi. The Guru didn't go; he sent his elder son, Ram Rai, a bright young man, to answer for the community. At court, tradition says, Ram Rai impressed everyone. Then came a hard question. Someone pointed to a line in Guru Nanak's long hymn, Asa di Var. In plain words, it says the clay of a Muslim's grave ends up in the potter's hands, kneaded into pots and bricks. It's a reflection on death: however a body is laid to rest, it becomes earth. The court heard it as an insult to Muslims. Ram Rai, wanting to please, said it had been copied wrong, and changed the word Muslim to a word meaning a faithless person. It worked. The court was satisfied. When the news reached Kiratpur, the gentle Guru, the one who sent medicine even to the emperor's son, was unmoved. Tradition says he declared that Ram Rai had turned his back on the Guru's word, and he never saw his son again. He passed over him and chose his younger son, Har Krishan, as Guru. Why so hard, from so soft a man? Because for Sikhs, the Gurus' word is not anyone's to trade, not even a Guru's son's. Gentleness with people and firmness about the word live in the same man: he would heal an emperor's son, but he would not let one word be edited to please a throne.

segments.voice: Bring to mind a promise you've made that's still open: to yourself, a friend, a child, or God if you pray. A small one is fine, like I'll call, I'll come, I'll stop, and notice any way you've been quietly rewording it, as in: I said I'd call, but a text counts. Then let the original words stand, as they were said.
Ram Rai. Guru Har Rai's elder son, who altered one word of Guru Nanak's hymn to please the emperor's court, and whom his father never saw again.
Your line: don't change the word. Tomorrow, the younger son he chose instead. That's day seventy-one.

72.title: A Guru at five
72.hook: the youngest Guru takes up the task as a small child and is remembered for his calm
72.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, in the daily Ardas, which says, in paraphrase, that at the sight of him all suffering departs, and honor him as a picture of calm wisdom in a child.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the changed word: Ram Rai shaded one word for the court, and his father never saw him again. Your line was don't change the word.

A five-year-old can tie a shoe, mostly. They can tell you, at length, about a dinosaur. They cry when the sandwich is cut the wrong way. Now put that child on a seat where grown men with long beards bow to him, and ask him to guide a whole community, while an older brother who thinks the job should be his watches, and an emperor wonders what kind of child this is. That was Har Krishan, the eighth Guru, chosen in 1661 when his father, Guru Har Rai, died.
screen: `A FIVE-YEAR-OLD.` → `BOWED TO BY GROWN MEN.` → `THE EIGHTH GURU.`

segments.voice: Guru Har Krishan became Guru at about five and lived only to about eight. So there are no great battles, and no hymns of his in the scripture. What Sikhs remember is his calm, and what came out of it. His older brother Ram Rai, the one who changed the word, went to the emperor Aurangzeb and pressed his claim, and the child Guru was summoned to Delhi. On the way, at a village called Panjokhara, tradition says a proud scholar challenged the boy: if you're really the Guru, explain the Gita, the great Hindu scripture, to me. The Guru didn't argue or show off. He asked for someone from the village, and a humble water-carrier named Chhajju was brought, a man who had never studied. The Guru touched him lightly with his stick, and Chhajju began to explain the Gita so deeply that the scholar was left silent, and humbled. Sikhs don't tell it as a trick. They tell it as wisdom that doesn't depend on age or schooling: the child Guru pointed away from himself, to the person the scholar least expected. In Delhi he stayed at the house of a Rajput noble, Raja Jai Singh. Tradition says the Raja's queen tested him by dressing as a maid among her servants, and the child walked straight to her. Tradition also says he declined to meet the emperor at all. Small, calm, unimpressed by the powerful. The youngest Guru.

segments.voice: Pick something ordinary: pour a glass of water, fold a shirt, wash a cup. Take three slow breaths, then do it at half speed, the way a small child does something important, feeling the weight of the cup and the sound of the water. When it's done, sit and let that calm spread into your breathing.
Chhajju. The water carrier whom the child Guru Har Krishan touched with his stick, so he could explain the Gita and humble a proud scholar.
Your line: small, and wise. Wisdom doesn't wait for age or schooling. Day seventy-two, done.

73.title: Smallpox in Delhi
73.hook: he nurses the sick during an epidemic in Delhi and dies of it at eight, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands
73.howItsDone: Visitors to Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi often take water from its pool home for the sick, and Sikhs remember Guru Har Krishan's care for the sick in the daily Ardas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Guru at five, and Chhajju the water-carrier who explained the Gita. Your line was small, and wise.

Empty streets. Door handles nobody wants to touch. Families keeping their distance from their own grandparents. And the people who went in anyway: nurses, cleaners, delivery drivers, neighbors carrying soup. In 1664, while the child Guru Har Krishan was staying in Delhi, an epidemic swept the city. Tradition names it smallpox, and some accounts add cholera. People were dying in the lanes. The eighth Guru was about seven, a guest far from home. He could have left.
screen: `A CITY WITH A SICKNESS LOOSE.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO WENT IN ANYWAY.` → `DELHI, 1664.`

segments.voice: Tradition says the young Guru did not hide. He went among the sick of Delhi, Hindu and Muslim alike, comforting and tending them, and his followers with him. The house where he stayed, Raja Jai Singh's bungalow, had a well, and tradition says the Guru blessed its water and gave it to the sick. People came in crowds. Then the child caught the disease himself. Sikhs tell of his last days with great tenderness. Burning with fever, he stayed calm. His frightened followers asked who would lead them after him. Tradition says the dying boy gave a short, puzzling answer: Baba Bakale. The Baba, the next Guru, is at Bakala, a village in Punjab. He said no more. That riddle is tomorrow's story, and the day after's. He died in Delhi in 1664, not yet eight years old. Here is what a visitor to Delhi can still see. The bungalow became Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, which still draws crowds. Beside it lies a large pool, fed, tradition says, from that same well, and people still take its water home to the sick. Its langar feeds great crowds. During the COVID-19 pandemic, gurdwaras in Delhi, Bangla Sahib among them, cooked and delivered meals to people who couldn't leave home. A child's service in one epidemic, echoing in another, more than three hundred and fifty years later.
screen: `AMONG THE SICK OF DELHI.` · `WATER FROM THE WELL.` · `BABA BAKALE.` · `GURDWARA BANGLA SAHIB TODAY.` · then, large: `HE SERVED THE SICK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is unwell right now, in body or in spirit: a friend in the hospital, a parent with a long illness, someone having a hard month. Hold them without trying to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for them; if you don't, just wish them ease, breath by breath.
Baba Bakale. The dying child Guru's riddle-answer about where to find the next Guru, at a village called Bakala in Punjab.
Your line: he served the sick. A frightened city, and a child who went toward it. Seventy-three days in.

74.title: The name of the sword
74.hook: Tyag Mal, youngest son of Guru Hargobind, fights so bravely he is called Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword
74.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, as both brave and deeply contemplative; his hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, often about detachment and calm, are sung in gurdwaras and at Sikh funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, smallpox in Delhi, and the child Guru's last words: Baba Bakale, the next Guru is at Bakala. Your line was he served the sick.

Some people get their names twice: once from their parents, and once from what they do. The kid everyone calls Doc because she bandaged the whole playground. The grandfather everyone calls Captain, though he never captained anything but the family. The second name tells you who a person became. The child Guru said the next Guru was at Bakala. To find out who he meant, the story goes back about thirty years, to Guru Hargobind's household and his youngest son, a quiet boy who got his second name on a battlefield. A name that means a sword, given to a man who would then spend twenty years in quiet.
screen: `NAMED TWICE.` → `GURU HARGOBIND'S YOUNGEST SON.` → `A NAME FROM A BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: He was born in Amritsar in 1621, and his parents named him Tyag Mal. Tyag means renunciation, letting go. Tradition remembers him as thoughtful, inward, drawn to quiet. Then came the battles of Guru Hargobind's later years, the ones from day sixty-eight. At the battle of Kartarpur, in 1635, the boy was about thirteen or fourteen. Tradition says he fought with such courage and skill with the sword that his father gave him a new name: Tegh Bahadur. Tegh is a sword. Bahadur means brave. Brave of the sword. You might expect a boy with that name to become a great commander. He did the opposite. After his father's death, he went with his mother, Mata Nanaki, and his wife, Mata Gujri, to Bakala, a village near the Beas where his mother's family lived. There, for about twenty years, he lived very quietly. Tradition says he spent long hours in meditation in a small room below ground, working with his hands and keeping to himself, while the Guruship passed to his nephew, Har Rai, and then to the child Har Krishan. People who met the grown man found someone gentle and still, who wrote hymns of calm detachment, some of them now in the Guru Granth Sahib. The boy they called brave of the sword spent those years in stillness at Bakala, making no claim. Tomorrow, someone comes to the village looking for him.

segments.voice: Let one moment come back when you were braver than you expected: you spoke up, you stayed, you walked into a room you dreaded. It doesn't have to be dramatic; feel it again in your body. Then notice how quiet that courage is now, sitting inside you, not needing to prove anything.
Tegh Bahadur. Brave of the sword, the name given to the boy Tyag Mal after he fought bravely at the battle of Kartarpur in 1635.
Your line: brave, then quiet. A sword for a name, and a quiet room for twenty years. That's seventy-four.

75.title: Twenty-two claimants at Bakala
75.hook: tradition says the trader Makhan Shah found the true Guru meditating in Bakala among many false claimants
75.tomorrow: journeys east and a new town
75.howItsDone: Sikhs retell the story of Makhan Shah finding Guru Tegh Bahadur at Bakala, and his cry 'Guru ladho re', the Guru is found, is remembered at the gurdwara in Baba Bakala.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the name of the sword: Tyag Mal became Tegh Bahadur, then went quiet at Bakala. Your line was brave, then quiet.

Search for almost anything online and a dozen people shout that they're the real one. The original recipe. The authentic brand. The only true expert. The loudest voice gets the top of the page. Now go to Bakala in 1664, after the child Guru's last words, Baba Bakale, reached Punjab. The next Guru is at Bakala. So, overnight, Bakala fills up with Gurus. Relatives of the Guru's family set up seats, gather followers, and announce themselves. Tradition says there were twenty-two of them. Somewhere in the village, a quiet man sits in a room below ground, saying nothing.
screen: `EVERYONE CLAIMS TO BE THE REAL ONE.` → `BAKALA FILLS WITH GURUS.` → `A QUIET MAN BELOW GROUND.`

segments.voice: The story Sikhs tell turns on Makhan Shah, a trader who shipped goods by sea. Tradition says his ship was caught in a terrible storm, and in his fear he vowed: if I reach land safely, I'll give five hundred gold coins to the Guru. The ship survived. He came to Punjab to keep his promise, and arrived in Bakala to find twenty-two Gurus. How do you choose? He had a quiet plan. He went to each claimant in turn, bowed, and laid down just two gold coins. Each one accepted the coins, blessed him, and thanked him. None of them knew about the vow. Then someone told him there was one more: a man who lived simply, meditating in a small room, and made no claim at all. Makhan Shah found Tegh Bahadur, bowed, and laid down two coins. Tradition says the quiet man looked up and said, gently: you promised five hundred. The merchant knew. He ran up onto the roof and shouted over the whole village, again and again: I've found the Guru! I've found the Guru! And so the man who had been brave, then quiet, became the ninth Guru. The real one wasn't the loudest. He wasn't even competing. He didn't tell Makhan Shah he was the Guru; he simply knew the truth of the man's heart. And the one who recognized him was not a scholar or a priest, but a trader who had kept his word.

segments.voice: Think of a question in your life where lots of voices are competing: a decision, a worry, a piece of news. Notice the loudest one and set it aside for a moment. Then listen for a quieter voice you've been walking past: a friend who said little, a feeling you haven't heard out, your own sense of what's true.

76.title: Journeys east and a new town
76.hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur travels as far as Assam and founds the town that becomes Anandpur
76.howItsDone: Sikhs visit Anandpur Sahib, the town founded by Guru Tegh Bahadur, and gurdwaras mark his travels in the east, from Patna and Dhaka to Dhubri in Assam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twenty-two claimants at Bakala, and Makhan Shah, the trader shouting from the roof. Your line was the guru is found.

Two suitcases and a rented shop in a new country. A cheap old house, fixed up one room at a time after a hard year. Starting over takes a kind of courage that isn't loud at all. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the new ninth Guru, did not have an easy welcome. Some of the disappointed claimants turned hostile; tradition says one of them even had a shot fired at him. So the quiet Guru did two things. He built a new home, and he set out on a long road east.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO STARTED OVER.` → `NOT AN EASY WELCOME.` → `A NEW HOME, AND THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the town. In 1665 the Guru bought land in the Shivalik foothills, near Kiratpur, from the ruling family of the hill state of Kahlur. He named the settlement Chakk Nanaki, after his mother, Mata Nanaki. It was rough ground by the river Sutlej, with hills behind. Over the years it would grow into a Sikh center known as Anandpur, the city of bliss. You met the word anand on day fifty-three, in the song of bliss. Much of the rest of this camp happens there. Second, the journey. Soon after founding the town, the Guru set out east, the way Guru Nanak had gone long before, visiting Sikh communities and holy places. He traveled through Agra and Allahabad, to Benares, and on to Patna, on the Ganges. There he left his wife, Mata Gujri, who was expecting a child, and kept going: to Dhaka, in Bengal, and all the way to Assam, in the far east, where tradition says he helped make peace between an imperial army and the Assamese kingdom. While he was far away, his son was born in Patna. The Guru would not see him for years. The quiet man from the room below ground didn't wait for a perfect life. He took rough land and started a town. He took the road and strengthened scattered communities. Build where you are, with what you have, and let it grow into something you may never fully see.

segments.voice: Think of something you've wanted to begin but keep saving for when life is calmer: a habit, a project, a friendship, a garden. If a seed, a pot or a notebook is near, you can even make that start now; if not, just hold the beginning.
Anandpur. The city of bliss that grew from Chakk Nanaki, the town Guru Tegh Bahadur founded near Kiratpur before journeying east as far as Assam.
Your line: build where you are. Rough ground was enough for a town. Day seventy-six.

77.title: The pandits of Kashmir
77.hook: Kashmiri Brahmins facing forced conversion come to him for help
77.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of the Kashmiri pandits coming to Anandpur as the beginning of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, and honor him as one who gave his life for the freedom of others to practice their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, journeys east and a new town: Chakk Nanaki, the town that became Anandpur. Your line was build where you are.

Spring of 1675, at Anandpur. The Guru is home, and his young son, Gobind Rai, is with him. A group of travelers arrives from the far north, from the valley of Kashmir, worn out from the mountain roads. They are pandits, Hindu Brahmin scholars and priests. They are not Sikhs. They've come a long way to ask a Guru for help.
screen: `ANANDPUR, 1675.` → `TRAVELERS FROM KASHMIR.` → `NOT SIKHS, ASKING FOR HELP.`

segments.voice: Here is what the pandits told the Guru, as Sikh tradition remembers it. Under the emperor Aurangzeb, the Mughal governor of Kashmir was pressing Hindus there to convert to Islam, and the Brahmins, as religious leaders, were under particular pressure. Tradition names their leader Pandit Kirpa Ram, from Mattan, near Anantnag. They had nowhere else to turn. Historians discuss how widespread this policy was, and how the court saw it; the sources are not all agreed. What the Sikh sources agree on is the scene at Anandpur, and three things stand out. First, the pandits were not the Guru's followers. They wore the sacred thread and the forehead mark, practices the Gurus themselves had not taken up. On day six you met Guru Nanak as a boy, refusing to wear it. Second, the Guru's own community was not being threatened in this request. He could have said: this isn't our fight. Third, the Guru listened. Tradition says he sat quietly for a long time, deep in thought, heavy with what they had told him. The question in the air was simple and terrible: who would stand up for the right of other people to practice a faith that wasn't his? His answer, and what it cost, come in the days ahead. Look back at this week: a word changed to please a court; a child Guru, calm before the powerful, who served the sick and died in Delhi; a boy renamed brave of the sword, who went quiet at Bakala; a trader shouting from a roof; a new town on rough ground. And now this: the people in need came to him, and he did not send them away.
screen: `PRESSURE TO CONVERT IN KASHMIR.` · `PANDIT KIRPA RAM LEADS THEM.` · `NOT HIS FOLLOWERS, NOT HIS THREAD.` · `THE GURU SITS AND LISTENS.` · `A WEEK OF QUIET COURAGE.` · then, large: `THEY CAME TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who came to you lately, even in a small way: a message you skimmed, a friend who said I'm fine too quickly, a coworker who needed more than they asked for. Replay it slowly, and this time just listen, without planning your answer, noticing what they were really asking. Stay with them, the way the Guru sat with the travelers.
Kirpa Ram. The Brahmin leader of the Kashmiri pandits who traveled to Anandpur in 1675 to ask Guru Tegh Bahadur for help.
